item.title: Brazil's presidential race heads to Lula–Bolsonaro run-off as right gains ground
item.dc:creator: Catherine Osborn
item.description: Now there are two: Brazil heads into a runoff after a first round that failed to fully energize voters, setting the stage for a more polarized contest that Washington is watching very closely.
item.content:encoded:
Brazil’s presidential race is heading to a runoff between left-wing President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and right-wing Senator Flávio Bolsonaro after neither candidate secured the more than 50% of valid votes needed to win outright.

The race was tight, with Flávio Bolsonaro finishing ahead of Lula in Sunday’s first-round election. With more than 99% of the vote counted, Bolsonaro secured more than 47% of the vote, while Lula came in second place with 45%.

If that sounds like déjà -vú, it’s because in many ways, this election is a rerun: Lula narrowly defeated Bolsonaro’s father, former right-wing President Jair Bolsonaro, in 2022. Jair Bolsonaro is now serving a 27-year prison sentence under house arrest after being convicted of plotting to overturn that election and prevent Lula from taking office.

Flávio has pledged to carry on his father’s legacy. Speaking to journalists and supporters outside his home in Brasília after the results came in, he said the vote showed Brazilians were ready for a political change.

“Brazil wants change, that’s the reading of what happened today,” Bolsonaro said. “It’s the end of the Workers’ Party era,” he added, referring to Lula’s political party.

Sunday’s results also pointed to a broader rightward shift in Brazilian politics, with the Bolsonaro camp performing strongly across the country.

Lula sought to rally his supporters in São Paulo, framing the next stage of the campaign as a fresh contest.

“Tomorrow we start a new campaign,” Lula said. “I am very good in the knockout stage. We will see who has the best plan.”

Lula also took aim at his opponent, warning voters about Bolsonaro’s political background. “On the other side we have an uncertainty with a biography of a dark past,” he said.

The presidential candidates who came in third, fourth, and fifth place are all right-wing, suggesting that Bolsonaro could have a natural pool of voters to draw from in the runoff. That could set the stage for another extremely tight contest on October 25.

Brazilians also chose governors and state and federal lawmakers Sunday, with early results showing that the right also made significant gains in Congress, particularly in the Senate. That could give Bolsonaro a stronger political base if he wins the presidency.

Lula, 80, is aiming for his fourth nonconsecutive term and has pledged to continue broad social spending and to stand up to Trump’s aggressive policies toward Latin America.

Bolsonaro, 45, pledges to slash the deficit and realign the country’s foreign policy with Washington. The result suggests Lula will now have to do more than defend his record: he will need to rebuild the broad coalition that returned him to power in 2022, including among younger voters who have shown less enthusiasm for his campaign.

This year’s presidential campaign featured smaller rallies compared to past years, perhaps because both of the candidates felt like known quantities to voters.

“I think the campaign feels more muted because people are tired of fighting,” said 38-year-old nutritionist Raysa Tavares after she voted Sunday afternoon in the Rio de Janeiro favela of Vidigal.

Businessman Caio Farias, 37, who voted in Rio’s upscale neighborhood of Leblon, said that he preferred other right-wing candidates to Bolsonaro, but voted for Bolsonaro in an effort to try to get the election over in one round.

Now, Brazilians are gearing up for another three weeks of campaigning. In the 2022 election, the second round of the election saw a sharp uptick in political violence, with dozens of people physically attacking each other for political reasons, Brazilian news site Pública reported.

Beyond the fact that this year’s contest features a younger Bolsonaro, there’s something else setting it apart from the last one: Trump is in the White House, with big ambitions for drawing politics in Latin America to the right. Lula has accused the United States of trying to meddle in Brazil’s election, which the U.S. State Department has denied.

Bolsonaro rallies have featured American flags and a giant inflatable doll of Trump holding a jailed Lula, while Lula has campaigned on the idea of protecting Brazilian sovereignty from foreign interference—a rarely-heard watchword in 2022. In Rio on election day, voters could be seen on the streets both with Trump T-shirts and “out with Trump” stickers.

The topic of Brazil’s relationship with the United States is sure to feature in second-round campaigning, as are domestic themes of security policy, corruption, and the economy, which polls say are top of voters’ minds.

But the first-round results have added another defining issue to the runoff: whether Brazil wants to continue with Lula or embrace the broader rightward shift that emerged from Sunday’s vote.

item.title: Jeffries says House Democrats reaching to flip Trump districts in attempt to repeat their 2018 sweep
item.dc:creator: LISA MASCARO
item.description: House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said Sunday his party is on track to win back control of the House, confident Democrats can overcome a fundraising disadvantage and reach deep into conservative areas to flip congressional districts won by President Donald Trump just two years ago.
item.content:encoded:
House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said Sunday his party is on track to win back control of the House, confident Democrats can overcome a fundraising disadvantage and reach deep into conservative areas to flip congressional districts won by President Donald Trump just two years ago.

In a conference call with reporters, Jeffries, who is in line to become House speaker if Democrats seize the majority, compared this midterm election to 2018, when Democrats swept to power during Trump’s first term in the White House.

“House Democrats are poised to take back the majority,” he said.

Jeffries, who is from New York, said that when Democrats took control of the House in 2018, most of the seats they flipped were in districts where Trump won in 2016.

“In 2026, we’re poised to do the same thing,” he said.

His comments were the latest display of confidence from Democrats with a month to go until the midterm elections on Nov. 3. The party is working to expand the map by going on offense in Republican-held districts, while Trump hits the trail in a red-state sprint to boost voter enthusiasm and shore up support from his base.

Republicans have a sizable cash advantage as House Speaker Mike Johnson steers the party closer to Trump to try to keep the majority. Trump is promising voters $5,000 cash dividends if the Republicans win, though it’s not at all certain that Congress would unleash the estimated $1 trillion-plus for such an outlay. Over the weekend, Trump announced $90 payments to seniors to help pay Medicare premiums.

Jeffries said Republicans are “failing and flailing.”

“The American people are not buying what MAGA Republicans are trying to sell,” he said.

With the House narrowly split, just a few seats could determine which party holds the gavel. Early voting is underway. Republicans are under pressure because of high gas prices stemming from the war with Iran.

Jeffries said a Trump-led redistricting effort to draw more favorable Republican districts in Texas, Florida and other states backfired in some places. At the same time, the House Democrats’ campaign arm announced late last week it was adding eight districts to its map of districts in play, including those in Kansas, Oklahoma, Virginia and Washington state.

“The Republican gerrymandering scheme has failed,” Jeffries said.

Jeffries cautioned, however, that “anything and everything” is possible, and urged Democrats to remain focused. “We can’t afford to take anything for granted,” he said.

Johnson, the Republican speaker, has been crisscrossing the country and insisted Republicans will be able to protect their majority. He stumped for Republicans in California last week and he is scheduled to be in more than 40 districts across some 20 states in the final weeks before November.

Jeffries, who was also in Western states over the weekend, said he too will be traveling in the weeks ahead.

item.title: Nolo changes from a hurricane to a typhoon after crossing the international date line
item.dc:creator: Associated Press
item.description: Nolo has changed from a strong hurricane to a typhoon after it crossed the International Date Line.
item.content:encoded:
Nolo has changed from a strong hurricane to a typhoon after it crossed the International Date Line.

Nolo was a Category 3 hurricane with maximum sustained winds of 115 mph (185 kph) Sunday morning Hawaii time before it crossed the agreed-upon line in the Pacific Ocean that separates one day from the next. Names of tropical cyclones vary by the parts of the world where they occur.

Monday morning Japan time, Typhoon Nolo had maximum sustained winds of 100 mph (162 kph) and was moving west at 19 mph (30 kph), according to the Japan Meteorological Agency.

“The good news is there’s a large, vast ocean, so even though it is still going to be strong, it’s not near any land,” said John Cangialosi, a senior hurricane specialist with the U.S. National Hurricane Center in Miami.

Tropical cyclones with winds over 74 mph (119 kph) are called hurricanes in the northern Atlantic Ocean and the central and eastern Pacific. They are typhoons in the North Pacific, while the South Pacific and Indian Ocean use just the generic term tropical cyclone no matter the strength of the storm.

Nolo is forecast to keep moving west and gradually weaken.

Nolo skirted Hawaii as a hurricane a week ago. It then lost some of its punch and became a tropical storm, before regaining hurricane strength on Friday.

Elsewhere in the Pacific, Hurricane Rachel continued heading westward on a path away from Mexico.

As the storm moved further out to sea, it was sending dangerous waves and swells back to the coast of west-central Mexico and the Baja California Peninsula, according to the hurricane center.

item.title: A proposed nickel mine near Gold Beach has a buyer, but years of studies remain
item.dc:creator: Theo Greenly
item.description: Homeland Nickel, a Canadian company pursuing a nickel mine near Gold Beach, has signed an agreement with a U.S. refiner to buy nickel from the site if the mine opens.
item.content:encoded:
Homeland Nickel, a Canadian company pursuing a nickel mine near Gold Beach, has signed an agreement with a U.S. refiner to buy nickel from the site if the mine opens.

The deal gives the proposed Red Flat mine a buyer, but years of feasibility studies and environmental reviews remain before mining could begin. Westwin Elements, the buyer, plans to build a full-scale refinery.

In a statement, Homeland said Westwin would buy roughly 20,000 metric tons of nickel concentrate a year under the agreement.

Homeland holds about 2,000 acres of mining claims at Red Flat, on federal land in the mountains about nine miles southeast of Gold Beach.

Red Flat is one of nine nickel properties Homeland holds in Southern Oregon. President and CEO Steve Balch said he estimates the properties together contain enough nickel to support mining for 50 to 60 years.

While the deal moves things forward, feasibility studies and environmental reviews still lie ahead. Balch said those would include studies of plant species, water drainage, and cultural or historical sites on the claims.

“These things would all have to be studied, and that’s not something that you do in one year,” Balch said.

Homeland also said exploration nearly 20 years ago identified cobalt at Red Flat, but the previous resource estimate did not disclose the metal.

“At the time, it wasn’t thought to have been of economic importance, and so it was never published in the original resource estimate,” Balch said. “But we have all that data, so in our updated resource, we’re adding cobalt to the nickel in terms of the two payables that the project would yield.”

Balch said the cobalt could increase the project’s gross revenue by as much as 15%.

Homeland expects to finish an updated estimate of the site’s nickel resources in November and a preliminary economic analysis in the first half of 2027.

Theo Greenly is a reporter with Jefferson Public Radio.

item.title: From Cuba to Portland: How puppeteer Yosmel López lost, then found, his purpose
item.dc:creator: Evan Rodríguez
item.description: In search of a better life in Oregon, López didn’t know whether he’d ever get back to the theater. But as it turns out, one special theater group needed him as much as he needed them.
item.content:encoded:
I’ve always been attracted to stories about starting over; hitting the reset button on your life, especially when it’s at a time that’s anything but convenient. I think there’s something very reassuring about this, because such stories remind us that it really is never too late to scrap whatever plan we thought we had a grip on and try something entirely different. So it’s no wonder that I was attracted to the story of Yosmel López.

I first met Yosmel (Yos for short) in the prep kitchen of a taqueria in NE Portland that I was filming a documentary back in 2024. At the time, he was still getting his bearings and learning how to navigate life in Portland, and in the US in general. Having just come from Guantanamo, Cuba, (the city, not the US Detention Center) only a year prior, there was a lot to process and grapple with. He found a society that doesn’t stop moving to let you catch your own breath, let alone learn the language, find a supportive community and pick up where he’d left off in a career that he had spent 15 years of his life building.

In Cuba, Yos was well established and internationally recognized as a puppet maker, theater director, and actor for children’s theater. He even got to travel to other countries to perform his plays, which is a rare privilege afforded to Cuban citizens as nearly everything must be approved by the state. The last show he worked on as a director dealt heavily with the topic of migration. After months of rehearsals, his own actors and friends began to emigrate from the island themselves. Sometimes the universe has a not-so-subtle way of delivering a message…

What I experienced while making this Art Beat story was an inside look at a niche style of theater for an important audience that arguably needs creative stimulation the most. It’s also a personal tale of resilience and determination that reunited Yos with his purpose and community at none other than the Milagro Theater, which in English translates to “miracle.”

item.title: Razor clam harvesting closed coastwide in Oregon due to high domoic acid levels
item.dc:creator: KLCC staff
item.description: The closure includes popular razor clam harvesting areas on Clatsop Beach.
item.content:encoded:
Razor clam harvesting is closed coastwide in Oregon as of Friday Oct. 2.

The announcement from the Oregon Department of Agriculture and the Oregon Department of Fish and Wildlife stated that domoic acid levels are above the safety threshold.

The closure includes popular razor clam harvesting areas on Clatsop Beach. Mussel harvesting on the south coast is now open, making mussel harvesting open coastwide. Bay clams and crabs are also open coastwide.

Domoic acid is a marine biotoxin. According to the Oregon Department of Fish and Wildlife, shellfish like razor clams feed on small plants in the water called phytoplankton that produce the toxin. When people eat contaminated shellfish, the toxin affect the digestive system, nervous system, or both.

Call the Shellfish Safety Hotline at 1-800-448-2474 for up-to-date information on shellfish harvests, or visit the ODA Recreational Shellfish Biotoxin Closures Webpage. To reopen an area for harvest, the ODA must collect two consecutive tests from an affected area with results below closure limits.

item.title: Eugene man turns 108: ‘As long as I’ve got my good mind, I can meet people’
item.dc:creator: Jireh Deng
item.description: Beryl Dillman reflects on more than a century of living and credits his longevity to a positive attitude, a healthy diet and no alcohol.
item.content:encoded:
Less than 1% of the world’s people can claim membership in the exclusive club of centenarians. One Eugene man has well surpassed that. He turned 108 on Thursday.

“Anybody who’s ahead of me in birthdays, raise your hand,” Beryl Dillman said, addressing a crowd that gathered in the dining hall of Merrill Gardens at Sheldon Park, an assisted living facility, to celebrate his birthday.

A few people chuckled, but no one could top him. “You don’t know what it’s like to be 100-plus. I’ve found out and I like it!” he said. Three large balloons overhead spelled out his age.

Dillman hummed contentedly as he took a bite of his white-frosted cake with the message in blue lettering, “Happy 108th Birthday Beryl.” The crowd cheered and clapped as 108 balloons were released from a balcony over his head. Posing for a photo, Dillman blew raspberries as he wiggled his fingers around his head and everyone laughed.

Dillman uses a walker to move around, but he’s still sharp and active. He likes to recite the alphabet backward and sing his favorite songs when he meets new people.

“As long as I’ve got my good mind, I can meet people,” Dillman said.

His family suspects that he’s one of the oldest people in Oregon.

A person at the celebration read aloud a letter from Gov. Tina Kotek, addressed to Dillman. “I didn’t even know who the governor was,” Dillman said. “That is so nice.”

Dillman has lived so long that he is participating in the New England Centenarian Study at Boston University, a research project documenting the oldest living people in the world. Dillman credits his diet for his longevity.

“Part of the secret is to be careful what you drink and eat,” Dillman said. “I never bothered with alcohol drinks and things like that.”

His daughter Ruth Sturges, 72, visits daily to take him on scenic car rides and to treat him to his favorite snack — a chocolate chip cookie and a cup of coffee.

“He’s always had such a positive attitude and a cheerful disposition,” Sturges said. “He’s always been a problem solver. So if there’s a stumbling block or barrier, he’s always looking for a way to fix it, not complain about it.”

Dillman, a retired educator, spent over 50 years as a principal and professor teaching at colleges in California and Illinois.

Sturges became teary-eyed as she described how her father showed his love for her in different ways when she was growing up. While she was in high school, he had prepared little gifts for her at every stop she made during a monthlong tour with a traveling choir.

“He was always very generous with his heart, with his time, with his humor,” Sturges said of her father’s approach to life and teaching.

Dillman was born in Indiana in 1918, the final year of World War I, the second-oldest of eight children. His earliest memories include riding a buggy with his grandparents and playing baseball in a church cemetery with his friends, using tombstones for bases.

Dillman had two daughters, six grandchildren and 19 great-grandchildren. One of his newest family members is the 6-month-old Bella Rose Sturges, who is still too young to sing “Happy Birthday” to her great-grandfather.

“She certainly has the very positive, cheerful outlook that he has,” Ruth Sturges said. Bella sucked quietly on a pacifier, observing the festivities with her piercing blue eyes. “She’s a great baby, never cries,” Sturges added.

Bella’s father, Philip Sturges, drove two hours from Portland with his daughter to celebrate with his grandfather. James Pence, another one of Dillman’s grandsons, had driven even farther — 5 ½ hours— from Yakima, Washington.

“It was worth the 11 hours to just even get to spend a couple hours with him,” Pence said. He said he rarely saw his even-keeled grandfather lose his temper over the years. “He was there to provide emotional and financial support through college and through having kids; it’s been a lifelong blessing.”

As medical advancements increase life expectancy, the number of centenarians living in the U.S. is expected to quadruple to over 400,000, according to the Pew Research Center. At Merrill Gardens, there are a few other seniors crossing the 100-year threshold, including Billie Marie Mitchell, 99, who turns 100 in November.

Mitchell said she can often hear Dillman, her neighbor two doors down, chuckling as he talks to his friends.

“He’s a colorful character,” Mitchell said. “He’s very friendly… he’ll always tell the truth. I think that’s a good quality.”

Jennifer Van De Hey, a director of the senior active living program at Merrill Gardens, said she loves to foster community and belonging among the residents to help them stay connected.

Van De Hey said assisted living is not a scary place when you have a good team. Every time a resident celebrates a birthday, she tries to make them feel special by blowing up the same number of balloons as their age. “Just to know that I brought joy to the residents, that day, makes my life so much more fulfilling,” Van De Hey said.

Dillman’s short-term memory is failing more these days, according to his daughter. She had to repeat certain questions to him so he could hear properly.

“Is there anything difficult about getting older?” his daughter asked him.

“Oh, anything good about getting older?” Dillman repeated the question to himself. “There’s bound to be some good to it.”

item.title: How the Cornell case is affecting women who have experienced sexual assault
item.dc:creator: Windsor Johnston
item.description: The rape allegations that have emerged from a Cornell University frat house are leading many women to remember their own experiences — and call for a wider reckoning over sexual violence.
item.content:encoded:
When Olivia Petter first saw the news about the sexual assault allegations at Cornell University, she was shocked by how familiar parts of the story felt for her.

“The more I found out, the more triggered I became,” she said. “I think for me, the worst thing was seeing the group messages that these boys were allegedly sending to each other on the night of the alleged rape.”

Reading those exchanges brought the London-based author back to boarding school in England, where she says older boys targeted her and her friends from the age of 13.

“They would walk past us and whisper ‘Fresh meat,’” Petter said. “They would rate us out of ten and shout numbers at us when we walked down to the dining hall.” Petter says she recalls boys pulling down girls’ trousers while they held their lunch trays, humiliating them in the school cafeteria.

After a party, when she was 17, she remembers a boy putting a “hand down my pants” when she was trying to go to sleep. “No preamble. We hadn’t been kissing... and I was kind of wriggling, trying to get him to stop.”

“The thing that people need to understand is when something like that happens to you, it’s really hard to just say, no, get off me, because your body goes into this panic mode,” she said. “You freeze and it takes a while for you to understand what’s happening.”

“There were just so many instances of sexual assault and we didn’t really recognize it at the time because we didn’t have the language,” she said, adding that the culture continued into her time at university.

Petter, now 32, is among those sharing their own experiences online in response to the recent rape allegations that have emerged at a Cornell University fraternity house.

A former Cornell student, identified as Jane Doe, sued the university and seven former students last month, alleging she was drugged and repeatedly raped at the Chi Phi fraternity house in October 2024, when she was 20 years old. Attorneys for some of the men have denied the accusations.

The case has led to a wider reckoning over attitudes to sexual violence. On social media, many women have been using the hashtag #IamJaneDoe to discuss their own experiences of sexual assault and rape.

Other universities have acknowledged the issue, too. As the case has become a national news story, the editorial board of The Daily Pennsylvanian — a student newspaper at the University of Pennsylvania — published a recent piece titled “Penn has a Cornell problem, too.”

For some survivors, following the coverage can feel like reliving an earlier assault, says Hannah Braunstein, a Washington D.C. based psychotherapist and trauma specialist. She says stories like these can bring back more than just memories for people who’ve been sexually assaulted.

“Suddenly, they’re inundated with all of this news and then their own experience through memories or body sensation is beginning to unfold for them. It can be absolutely horrifying,” Braunstein said. “And it can immediately transport them back in time.”

For Erin Smith that reaction was immediate. The yoga instructor and mindfulness coach, who lives in Winchester, Ky., first saw the news about Cornell on social media and immediately searched for more details.

“I was so enraged, I set my phone down and just paced around my kitchen like a caged tiger,” Smith recalled. She says the story brought back the physical distress she remembered from being assaulted as a child.

“I had that feeling in my stomach that happened during my experience [when] I was 12,” said Smith, who is now 53.

Braunstein says repeated exposure to stories like these can intensify emotions. Yet, people may feel compelled to keep reading, hoping more information will help them feel better.

“We keep searching for more information because we think if we understand every detail, then finally we’ll feel better internally,” she said. “But, often it does the opposite, and keeps people activated internally.”

Braunstein recommends using a timer to keep news or social media checks to five minutes a day. When someone feels overwhelmed, she suggests turning their attention to their immediate surroundings.

“One thing I talk about with clients in my office is using first sight, looking around the room and calling out what you see, noticing what you hear,” she said. “Feeling your feet on the floor. That’s a grounding technique that works.”

Smith said she eventually recognized that she needed a break from the comments on social media. Spending time outside, being with her dog and playing guitar has helped her feel calmer. But, she said the anger remains, so she has started to write about it.

Petter also turned to writing. As she continues following the case, she wants to use her anger to start a dialogue around sexual assault.

“I want to hold on to the rage because I think rage is powerful and will enable me to have these conversations with the people in our lives,” she said. “And when I say people, I mean men.”

Petter says she wants men to have those conversations among themselves, too, and challenge derogatory comments about women within their own friend groups, including online.

For Smith, the Cornell case feels personal because it brings so many survivors of sexual assault back to their own experiences.

“I think that’s why so many women are triggered right now, because Jane Doe is all of us.” she said. “We all have some sort of story.”

item.title: How the Coquille Indian Tribe is working to restore Chinook and protect its traditions in Southern Oregon
item.dc:creator: Theo Greenly
item.description: To rebuild the Coquille River’s struggling run, the tribe and state are removing invasive predators and raising young salmon.
item.content:encoded:
William Murphy wears sunglasses and a woven cedar baseball cap over his long gray hair as he stands beside the charcoal pit he’s helped man for 19 years. The tribal elder says the Ko-Kwel Salmon Celebration is his chance to share Coquille Indian culture with the broader community.

“We’re highlighting our gift of the magnificent way we can produce cooked fish, and we’re trying to share that with the public,” Murphy said.

Traditional canoes, the Miluk language, Native crafts, songs and acorn mush connect the celebration to the Coquille homeland. The tribe describes the nearby Coquille River as a focal point of its life since time immemorial.

One of the few things not from the Coquille River is the salmon.

“We kind of don’t have the opportunity to provide our own fish, or we would,” Murphy said.

The festival requires roughly half a ton of salmon — more than the struggling Coquille River run can provide. Instead, the tribe purchased fish from tribes along the Columbia River.

‘We are now memories and thoughts’

Commercial salmon fishing had been declining for decades before the Coquille’s Chinook returns crashed. Coos Bay was once a major salmon port. In 1970, it handled more than half of Oregon’s South Coast salmon landings.

“It used to be hundreds and hundreds and hundreds of these wooden plank boats,” Murphy said.

The fleet shrank over the following decades as salmon runs and fishing opportunities declined.

“We disappeared. We went away,” Murphy said. “We are now memories and thoughts.”

The salmon troll fleet dwindled slowly. The Coquille River’s Chinook run collapsed much more quickly.

Starting around 2018, salmon returns in many of Oregon’s coastal rivers crashed.

“There was a sharp drop-off, kind of coast wide, and over the next couple of years, other coastal basins recovered,” said Ed Hughes, the Oregon Department of Fish and Wildlife’s acting fish district biologist in Charleston. “But in the Coquille here, they didn’t bounce back.”

Hughes said the Coquille’s failure to rebound helped biologists connect the decline to invasive smallmouth bass, which prey on young salmon. Warmer river temperatures, low flows and changing ocean conditions have also hurt salmon survival.

The state wildlife agency brought its concerns to the tribal council, said Brenda Meade, chair of the Coquille Indian Tribe.

“We talked a lot about what the issues were and how we were going to fix it,” Meade said.

In 2022, the tribe and the state formalized a co-management agreement covering fish and wildlife across five southwest Oregon counties.

Their work has included removing invasive bass, improving the collection of adult salmon for breeding and expanding hatchery efforts. In 2022, they also developed a conservation hatchery program to rebuild the Coquille’s wild fall Chinook population.

Tribal co-management

A few days after the celebration, tribal fisheries workers gathered at Ferry Creek in Bandon. They waded into the creek and stretched a seine net across the water, pushing hundreds of finger-sized salmon smolts downstream.

Jesse Rodriguez, a fisheries technician with the tribe’s natural resources department, had been standing in the creek in rubber waders all day.

The fish are spawned at Bandon Hatchery, raised at Cole Rivers Hatchery and then brought back to Ferry Creek to acclimate.

“They get the scent of the river, and then they’re ready to go out to the ocean,” Rodriguez said. “So we’re trying to just kind of make sure we can get as much out to the ocean without any harm.”

The goal is for the young salmon to imprint on Ferry Creek and return as adults after spending a few years in the ocean. Some can then be collected for breeding to produce another generation.

“I definitely think that the work that we’re doing here is going to make a difference. We’re putting a lot of fish into the river,” Rodriguez said. “We’re just trying to basically jump-start this whole population of salmon.”

And now, there are signs of progress.

Meade said fish from the tribe’s earlier releases are beginning to return.

“This year is so important because that four-year rotation of the smolt that we were a part of releasing for the first time are now the fish that are coming back into the river,” Meade said.

That doesn’t mean Coquille River salmon have recovered. The tribe is still trying to rebuild a run from near extinction.

For Meade, the work underscores the importance of traditional knowledge and Indigenous stewardship.

“The salmon were not going to be able to be healthy again without the Coquille Tribe in the water with them,” Meade said. “Those are our salmon.”

Restoring the run also means protecting the salmon at the heart of the tribe’s ceremonies, traditions and teachings.

“I couldn’t live in a world that there were no salmon in the Coquille River,” she said.

item.title: Powwow dancing isn’t always accessible. This Puyallup Tribe dad wants to change that
item.dc:creator: Owen Henderson
item.description: Providing disability accommodations for powwow participants isn’t very common on the powwow circuit, but one man has made it his mission to bring the practice to dances across North America.
item.content:encoded:
Providing disability accommodations for powwow participants isn’t very common on the powwow circuit, but one man has made it his mission to bring the practice to dances across North America.

“ I saw the need to fulfill something that is genuine to my heart,” said Puyallup Tribe member Shawn Reynolds. “And that is offering time on the floor for individuals with special needs, autism, Down syndrome, and any other special needs, as well as disabilities.”

In many respects, the Fourth Annual South Sound Powwow in Graham, Wash., was nothing out of the ordinary.

On a late-September afternoon, a procession began a slow march across the Bethel High School gym, with a steady drumbeat and a commanding voice that rang out across the floor. It was led by a beadwork-laden man carrying a staff adorned with eagle feathers. A contingent of veterans wearing cedar-woven hats held national, state, and tribal flags. They were followed by the powwow’s head dancers — a young man in a beaded chest plate and feathered roach, and two young women in jingle dresses strung with conical bells.

But two less conventional figures rounded out this procession, Shawn’s sons Nakotah and Dakotah Reynolds of the Puyallup and Otoe-Missouria Tribes. It’s often required to wear all the appropriate regalia to go out on the powwow floor. But these 11-year-old twin boys wore T-shirts, shorts, beaded headbands, and matching stoles. One boy had a pair of noise-dampening headphones clamped around his ears.

Nakotah and Dakotah have autism. Wearing all the customary regalia — and much of the powwow environment itself — can be overstimulating for them.

“ All the noise, all the drumming, the colors, the bells, the stomping, all of that can be triggering,” Shawn said.

Both boys also hold royalty titles from a powwow in April, entitling them and their family to sponsor a “special”, a dance of their choosing, at a powwow within the next year. And that gave their dad an idea.

“I’ve been doing powwows for a really long time, most of my life,” Shawn said. “One of the things that I don’t see is categories, or specials, for our individuals with disabilities or special needs.”

Shawn set out to change that four months ago. He reached out to South Sound Powwow directors Rachel Barger and Grace Leatham with a pitch — hold a special where dancers of all ages and all abilities could join the dancing, using whatever accommodations they needed.

“ I danced in my school district powwow growing up, and it wasn’t ever something we included,” Leatham said.

Leatham, who is Tsimshian and Blackfeet, is a Bethel High School Native American Education teacher.

“I know we had special needs students in our programs, but I didn’t see them ever participating in our powwow classes or our powwow itself,” Leatham said. “I just felt like it was really important to bring that accessibility in.”

After several hours of dancing, drumming, and singing, Shawn stepped up to the front of the gym to explain his special to the crowd.

“ You can come down with your blankets, your tablets, your headphones,” he said. “You don’t have to be in regalia. You can have your caregivers with you. You can have your parents with you, a support person or persons.”

While some powwows have competitive dance categories and most categories are limited by age or dance style, the same doesn’t have to be true of specials. So, Shawn told participants to dance however they wanted.

“You can do the worm,” he said. “You can do whatever you’ve got to do. I just want to see you come touch the dance floor … I wanted to give you guys a safe space to come down here and participate in your culture.”

Nakotah and Dakotah stepped out to the center of the gym. They were accompanied by their sisters, Cheyenne and Kailee. A drum struck up a beat, slower and smoother than some of the previous songs. Cheyenne, who also has autism, began to twirl and step to the rhythm, the purple ribbons on her shawl swaying and arcing through the air.

“It’s kind of like creating medicine when you spin … It’s like you’re about to dance with ancestors,” Cheyenne said. “ It feels like you’re not the only one just dancing out there who is autistic.”

A crowd filtered down from the bleachers and gathered on the floor, including elders, young adults and kids alike. Some held the arm of a family member as they moved around in a circle. Some, like Nakotah, wore headphones. Many wore bits and pieces of regalia, or street clothes alone.

Among them was Hadlee, a young Sioux Nation descendant, who was born with a heart condition called Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome. Her mother, Aundrea Carmichael, said she was worried when Hadlee was younger that the condition would limit her physical ability. But on the floor that day, Hadlee moved with the circle.

“It was so touching to see her actively participate physically today in this dance culture,” Carmichael said. “ Intuitively, she followed the beat, she moved her feet, and she knew exactly what to do. It was really touching to see. It was really impressive and incredible to be included in.”

Shawn now aims to spread this idea to other powwow organizers and provide spaces for all to participate.

“ My plan is to try and get powwows across the country, both in the U.S. and Canada, to incorporate not only specials, but a full dance category specifically catering to our individuals with special needs and disabilities,” Shawn said.

“ I know I can’t be the first person to do something like this,” he said. “But I don’t want to be the last.”

Owen Henderson is a reporter with KUOW.

item.title: Atkinson and Legree team for big passing day in Oregon State's 56-26 win in Pac-12 opener
item.dc:creator: Associated Press
item.description: Braden Atkinson threw five touchdown passes, three to Jesse Legree, and Oregon State defeated Colorado State 56-26 on Saturday in a Pac-12 opener for both teams.
item.content:encoded:
Braden Atkinson threw five touchdown passes, three to Jesse Legree, and Oregon State defeated Colorado State 56-26 on Saturday in a Pac-12 opener for both teams.

Atkinson found Legree down the right sideline for a 50-yarder to open the scoring. Legree turned a short pass into a 38-yard score to make it 38-14 at halftime. Legree’s 53-yard run-and-catch made it 56-26 with nine minutes remaining in the game.

Legree finished with 157 yards on five receptions. Legree, who had 240 yards in a 35-24 loss to Texas Tech on Sept. 12, became the third Beaver to reach 100 yards receiving in five straight games, joining Mike Haas (2005) and Brandin Cooks (2013).

Atkinson completed 31 of 34 passes for 428 yards, going over 300 yards for the fifth straight game, trailing only Sean Mannion, who had seven straight for Oregon State in 2013.

Oregon State (3-2, 1-0) outscored Colorado State 42-12 after the Rams had tied it 14 following a Beavers fumble early in the second quarter.

K’saan Farrar was 16-of-26 passing for 165 yards with a rushing and passing TD for the Rams (2-3, 0-1). Reginald Vick Jr. had 99 yards receiving.

Up next

Oregon State: home against San Diego State next Saturday.

Colorado State: home against San Jose State on Oct. 12.

item.title: The Supreme Court faces another term jam-packed with controversy
item.dc:creator: Nina Totenberg
item.description: The Supreme Court term opens on Monday with big test cases on religion, guns and climate change. Plus, the emergency docket keeps popping.
item.content:encoded:
The U.S. Supreme Court formally opens a new term on Monday, with big test cases on religion, bans on semi-automatic weapons, climate change, immigration and — waiting in the wings — election law cases.

It used to be that the first Monday in October marked the beginning of a new Supreme Court term. And that’s still true, technically. But for all practical purposes, the formerly quiet summer months after the court finishes its opinions in all argued cases no longer exists.

Indeed, as Georgetown University law professor Stephen Vladeck observes, the number of emergency appeals has ballooned during the Trump administration, while at the same time, fully briefed and argued cases have dropped precipitously over the years.

“So now we have twice as many full court rulings on emergency applications as we have on the merits docket,” Vladeck observes, adding, “That is a very new phenomenon.”

The difference is that decisions on the emergency docket are rendered quickly, with little briefing, no oral arguments, and ultimately little or no explanation of the ruling. In contrast, a decision on the merits is typically worked on for months after full briefing and lengthy oral arguments.

Of late, the court seems to be making an effort to offer some limited explanations of its emergency docket rulings, but lower court judges, both liberal and conservative, complain that isn’t enough to provide them with adequate guidance. And the Trump administration often takes what used to be the rare step of getting to the Supreme Court by leapfrogging over lower appellate courts that the administration views as hostile.

With that backdrop, here are the cases the court will be hearing in the coming weeks:

Climate change

The opening case, to be argued Monday, tests whether state and local governments can sue energy companies for allegedly deceiving the public about the damaging effects of fossil fuels.

“The theory is that the energy company defendants deceived the public for many years,” says Deepak Gupta, who teaches at Harvard Law School and practices law in Washington, D.C. What the companies were telling the public for years, he says, is “the opposite of what the company’s own scientists knew, and the local cost of that deception.”

That said, however, most court observers see the case as an uphill battle for environmentalists.

Religion

Perhaps the biggest case of the term so far, in terms of ripple effects, involves religion, a subject on which the court’s conservative super majority has dramatically changed its legal doctrine. Indeed for the better part of a century, the Supreme Court emphasized the First Amendment’s separation of church and state, with the free exercise of religion playing an important — but secondary — role. Since President Trump’s appointment of three new justices, however, things have changed.

“It’s literally the opposite of what the law was not that long ago, and it’s just a complete shift,” observes Michigan State University law professor Frank Ravitch.

The court may, in fact, be on the verge of requiring taxpayers to fund religious schools that refuse to admit LGBTQ students and parents. Last term the justices deadlocked on the issue in a separate case after Justice Amy Coney Barrett recused herself because of a conflict. The 4-4 tie vote automatically left in place an Oklahoma Supreme Court decision that barred overtly religious charter schools from from being funded by the taxpayers. But this year the issue is back in a case from Colorado. The case centers on a state law that provides universal preschool programs that are open to all students, regardless of race, ethnicity, religious affiliation, sexual orientation or gender identity.

St. Mary Catholic Parish in Littleton, Colo., wants the state funding guaranteed in the state’s universal pre-k law. But it doesn’t want to admit LGBTQ students or students with gay or trans parents. The parish maintains such admissions would violate church’s right to the free exercise of religion. The state counters that funding the church school would violate the state’s anti-discrimination law.

The court’s conservative majority has, in multiple cases, ruled in favor of religious exemptions from generally applicable laws. Until now, however, the court has never said that religious schools are entitled to full taxpayer funding. But given the current court’s views, and with Justice Barrett participating in the Colorado case, taxpayers could well end up having to fund religious schools in Colorado and elsewhere.

Bans on semi-automatic weapons

In December the court will hear a case testing whether state and local governments violate the Second Amendment right to bear arms when they ban semi-automatic weapons, like the AR-15.

Former Solicitor General Don Verrilli Jr., articulates two different ways to look at the question.

On the one hand the AR-15 “can deliver upwards of 100 bullets per minute” without any enhancements, and 500 bullets per minute with various enhancements. On the other hand, he notes that millions of Americans own AR-15s, “and it would be quite disruptive to suggest all these Americans ... would be dispossessed of their weapons.”

Lawyer Erin Murphy, who has litigated lots of cases on behalf of gun owners, says the “single most important question is who gets to decide what guns you have,” and he argues it makes no sense to say, “You’ve got this right against the government, but the government decides which arms you can get.”

Immigration

The Trump administration has repeatedly taken positions in immigration cases that no other administration has adopted. Most recently, the court announced it would hear arguments and decide a case testing whether the Department of Homeland Security may deport migrants to so-called “third countries,” when their countries of origin refuse to accept them. Since Trump began his second term, his administration has deported thousands of people to third world countries where they have no connections, may not speak the language, have often been jailed and allegedly subject to torture. The court has twice blocked lower court decisions that prevented the third country policy, and now the justices have said they will hear arguments about the policy in December.

In a second immigration case, the issue is the Trump administration’s policy of detaining undocumented immigrants without a bond hearing, regardless of how long they have been in the U.S.

Possible cases: The 10 commandments and much more

There are many more cases waiting in the wings that the justices may take up. Among them is a case that seeks to reverse a nearly half-century-old Supreme Court precedent; it bars public schools from posting the Ten Commandments in public school classrooms. Now, however, Texas, Arkansas, Louisiana and Alabama have passed laws that conflict with the Supreme Court’s 1980 ruling, and the lower courts are split on the question. That split all but guarantees the the Supreme Court will revisit the question.

Another case that could to make it to the court this term tests whether states can regulate Kalshi, the $40 billion prediction market behemoth that has sports fans betting on everything from the next pitch to the point spread or at the other end of the spectrum, betting on the outcome of Supreme Court cases.

And then there are cases that the Trump administration has slow-walked for close to two years, after quickly losing in the lower courts. Prime examples are the administration’s attempt to deny medical research grants to Harvard University, and other attempts to deny security clearances to law firms, as well as seeking money damages from law firms Trump views as hostile. Earlier this year the Justice Department told a federal court in Washington that it was dropping the law firm cases. But the next day it went back to court to reverse course.

“They don’t want to take up cases that they’re going to lose, but on the other hand, they have a boss who wants everything taken up there [to the Supreme Court],” says Stanford University law professor Pam Karlan.

Georgetown’s professor Vladeck adds that in his view, “The real story of the upcoming term hasn’t been written yet because what we’re going to look back on as the biggest cases of the term … are not on the docket yet.”

Elections

More immediately, the probability is that like it or not the justices will be drawn into the election. The Trump administration has sought to influence elections in numerous ways, and it’s unclear what efforts the administration might take going forward.

Democrats have a battalion of lawyers lined up to deal with problems on the ground — whether it’s moving polling places at the last minute or having federal agents stationed near polling places. But if there are serious voting problems, they will likely end up at the Supreme Court’s door — on the emergency docket.

item.title: Coast Guard searching for missing medical plane carrying 6 people
item.dc:creator: Frank Langfitt
item.description: Flight data shows the jet dropped at least 9,000 feet over two minutes, then leveled off for several more minutes, before disappearing.
item.content:encoded:
The U.S. Coast Guard is searching the waters south of Nantucket, Mass., for a Canadian air ambulance that disappeared early Saturday while traveling from Bermuda to Boston.

The Gulfstream G100 is believed to have been carrying six people on board when it lost contact with air traffic control, according to the Coast Guard.

Flight data shows the jet dropped at least 9,000 feet over two minutes, then leveled off for several more minutes, before disappearing. The pilot declared an emergency, according to Nantucket Memorial Airport. During an exchange, air traffic control asked the pilot of the air ambulance, “You’re coming in blind?”

A fire rescue dispatcher warned emergency crews to prepare for the planes’ arrival. She said it was 15 minutes away, suffering from electrical issues and had lost radio and radar, according to audio on Broadcastify and reviewed by The Boston Globe.

The Coast Guard has deployed two search and rescue planes as well as a helicopter and a motor lifeboat.

The plane is operated by Latitude Air Ambulance, based in Ontario, Canada. The company website says it has run thousands of missions since 2009 returning patients and loved ones to their families back home. The firm boasts “a flawless safety record.”

The website says the air ambulances are staffed by two pilots and a medical team and include a stretcher as well as full ICU medical equipment and supplies.

item.title: The Archive Project - Annie Dillard
item.description: This week, we’re reaching way back into our archive to feature a talk from Pulitzer Prize winning writer Annie Dillard’s special event in 1989.
item.content:encoded:
When Annie Dillard won the Pulitzer Prize in 1975, she was the youngest women ever to do so. She won for a book published the previous year called “Pilgrim at Tinker Creek,” which is a nonfiction book that meditates on writing, solitude, the natural world, and spirituality. The book had a profound impact at the time of its publication and garnered comparisons to Henry David Thoreau’s Walden.

Dillard has gone on to have genre bending career, publishing over a dozen titles including book-length nonfiction, novels, essays, and criticism, in addition to more than 25-years of teaching at universities in the Pacific Northwest and the east coast. In 2015 she was awarded the National Humanities Medal for her life’s work.

In this talk, her characteristic sense of irony and humor elicits huge laughs from the audience and her generous spirit invites quiet attention when she tells a story. She reads two excerpts -- first from “Pilgram at Tinker Creek” and then from a book of essays called “Teaching a Stone to Talk.” Whether she is describing muskrats in Virginia or witnessing an eclipse in the Yakima Valley, she draws profound insights into the nature of existence and what the natural world has to tell us about ourselves.

Bio:

Annie Dillard is born in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania in 1945, in a poet and author best known for her prose in both fiction and nonfiction. Dillard has been considered a major voice in American literature since she published “Pilgrim at Tinker Creek” in 1974 and won a Pulitzer Prize. Influenced by Henry David Thoreau and Walt Whitman, Dillard writes compressed, lyric poetry and prose that engages the balance of daily life within the frame of literature and ideas.

Dillard’s numerous books include the poetry collections “Tickets for a Prayer Wheel” and “Mornings Like This: Found Poems,” the nonfiction books “Pilgrim at Tinker Creek,” “An American Childhood,” “For the Time Being,” and “The Abundance: Narrative Essays Old and New,” and the novels “The Living” and “The Maytrees.”

A member of the American Academy of Arts & Sciences and a Fellow of the American Academy of Arts and Letters, Dillard also holds honorary doctorates at Boston College, the University of Hartford, and Connecticut College. Additional honors include grants from the National Endowment for the Arts and the John Simon Guggenheim Foundation, a New York Press Club Award for Excellence, an Appalachian Gold Medallion, a Campion Award, and an Academy Award in Literature from the American Academy of Arts and Letters. She received the National Endowment for the Humanities Medal in 2014, awarded to her by President Barack Obama.

item.title: Benson High School student faces domestic terrorism charges in chemical spill incident
item.dc:creator: Joni Land
item.description: The Multnomah County District Attorney’s Office will seek to try the 15-year-old as an adult.
item.content:encoded:
Note: This story contains a description of suicide. If you or someone you know may be considering suicide, contact the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline by dialing 988, or the Crisis Text Line by texting HOME to 741741.

A 15-year-old Benson Polytechnic High School student is facing multiple felony charges, including domestic terrorism, after allegedly releasing toxic chemicals inside the school last month.

Multnomah County District Attorney Nathan Vasquez said in a Friday press conference that his office will seek to try the child as an adult.

The teenager will face 19 charges total, a Multnomah County Circuit Court spokesperson told OPB.

Those charges include:

  • One count of domestic terrorism in the first degree
  • One count of domestic terrorism in the second degree
  • 10 counts of attempted aggravated murder
  • One count of attempted murder in the first degree
  • One count of attempted murder in the second degree
  • Unlawful manufacturing a destructive device
  • Unlawful possession of a destructive device
  • Possession of a weapon in a public building
  • Unlawful use of a weapon
  • Reckless endangering of another person

The student arrived for his initial appearance at the Multnomah County Juvenile Justice Center on Friday. The small courtroom was packed with his family members, reporters and representatives from the District Attorney’s office and the Portland Police Bureau.

The student entered the courtroom wearing a blue button-up shirt, jeans and slip-on shoes. He spent most of the hearing quietly observing his surroundings. Stuffed animals and children’s books decorated the front of the judge’s bench.

OPB is not disclosing the student’s name because he is a minor and has not been convicted.

In court, Deputy District Attorney Eric Zimmerman described the events leading up to the alleged attack: how the student arrived at school wearing gloves and goggles. He allegedly attempted to combine different chemicals inside the school, eventually passing out as a cloud billowed from the concoction.

He said the student attempted to make hydrogen sulfide, which is toxic. Multiple staff members and students reported trouble breathing and headaches.

Zimmerman said the student had written extensively on social media about feelings of suicide and his desire to hurt fellow students. Police found multiple dangerous chemicals. He also said that, on Friday morning, officials with the FBI had found numerous references on the student’s devices to 764, an extremist group that officials say works to exploit minors online into committing violent crimes.

Joe Mitacek, vice principal at Benson High, also addressed the court and said the school is still feeling the impact.

“The impact of our student body has been one of terror,” Mitacek said. “It’s been hard to get kids to return to school.”

At the later press conference, Vasquez said that if teachers and staff had not acted quickly to remove students from the situation, the end result could’ve been much worse.

“I’m a firm believer in compassion and accountability and being empathetic, but those two things are not mutually exclusive,” Vasquez said. “We can have empathy, but we also must make sure that we have an accountable system that makes sure that our students and our schools are safe going forward.”

Attorneys for the student denied all the allegations, and said in a statement Friday that the boy is “receiving appropriate and necessary mental health treatment.”

“Unlike the adult criminal system, juvenile court is structured to prioritize the individual needs of young people and to promote rehabilitation and healing,” the attorneys wrote. “The family is grateful that no one else was injured and for the swift intervention of school staff and first responders. They ask for privacy at this time so they may focus on their child’s recovery.”

At the hearing, Juvenile Hearings Referee Kristine Almquist said the student would be released to the Parry Center for Children in Portland, where he’s been receiving mental health treatment.

Zimmerman requested a hearing to reconsider Almquist’s decision in front of a judge, which is set for next Tuesday.

item.title: Bike buses give Portland commuters a ‘more fun’ way around the I-5 closure
item.dc:creator: Lillian Karabaic
item.description: The Portland Bureau of Transportation offers weekly group rides as an alternative commute during the southbound closure of Interstate 5.
item.content:encoded:
As the Interstate 5 southbound closures through Portland’s Rose Quarter continue to disrupt metro area commutes, some people are getting to work on two wheels — together.

They say it helps create a sense of community, a sense of safety and relief that they’re not caught in traffic.

Every Wednesday through Oct. 14, the Portland Bureau of Transportation is running special bike buses from North and Northeast Portland to downtown. The rides are part of the city’s effort to give people alternatives during the closure, and to encourage biking as a transportation option.

The city’s broader bike bus program began in 2024 as an internal program for city employees. It was initially planned as a single Bike Month event, but proved popular enough that the city continued monthly rides through October. In 2025, the program opened to the public. This year, city staff and community volunteers have both served as ride leaders.

The bike buses operate primarily on Portland’s neighborhood greenways, traveling at a leisurely pace and picking up riders at designated time points. All of the routes converge in downtown Portland at Salmon Street Springs at 8:15 a.m.

The weekly rides during the I-5 closure are a special edition; the other six routes are still only happening once a month. The goal was to focus on the neighborhoods most affected by the I-5 southbound closure.

Creating community and safety

Karin Wohlert, who works downtown, already commutes by bike regularly. She said the I-5 closure has made her especially grateful not to be sitting in traffic.

“I see the traffic. I’m just happy that I’m not down there,” Wohlert said.

She began joining the bike buses this summer and thinks it “creates great community and it also creates safety.”

That sense of safety can be especially important for less experienced riders — including the youngest participant on the Sept. 30 bike bus.

Aiden Forsi joined the group with 4-year-old Conor. The two normally take the same route to school and join the bike bus when they encounter it.

“This is just kind of happenstance,” Forsi said. “This is our normal route to school. So when we see it, we stop, and when it’s not here, we just keep going.”

Forsi said other riders helped keep Conor protected when they first joined the bike bus.

“It’s good vibes,” he said.

Multi-modal commute options

Not everyone on the bike bus was using it for their entire commute.

Abby McFeeters-Krone leads a connecting bike bus to Nike’s campus. McFeeters-Krone said the group gives people an opportunity to try biking to work in a supportive environment.

“I just like giving new riders the opportunity to kind of see what it’s like to bike into work,” McFeeters-Krone said. “Ideally, it would be a comfortable space to try it for the first time.”

“This is a broader effort with our company to get more people to bike in. This seemed like a good opportunity to take advantage of what the city’s already doing and have a meeting place.”

The bike bus to the Beaverton campus is often multi-modal, combining biking with riding the MAX light rail. Florin Veja works with McFeeters-Krone and said he normally bikes from Vancouver, Washington, to Beaverton. He said he also sometimes combines biking with MAX.

The Sept. 30 Northeast Portland route was his first time joining a city bike bus.

“I just wanted to experience it and join my colleague,” Veja said.

‘More fun than sitting in traffic’

Jack Gordon regularly volunteers as a bike bus leader on the East Portland Community Center route. He joined the special Sept. 30 northeast bike bus because he had the morning off and wanted to go on a ride.

Gordon doesn’t work downtown. He said he participates because he enjoys the social aspect.

“I just think it’s really nice and fun to get out in the morning and be with other people,” he said.

For people who are nervous about joining a group ride, Gordon said the bike buses are intentionally low-pressure and participants ride slowly.

“I think that it’s a lot less serious than people think it will be,” he said. “It’s really fun to see everybody come together and just having a good time in the morning. It’s so much more fun than sitting in traffic.”

PBOT has added a few features specifically for the I-5 closure bike buses. The north and northeast routes have live GPS tracking so riders can see where the bike bus is in real time. And riders can receive $5 in market currency for the Shemanski Park Farmers Market as an incentive for changing their commutes.

The weekly rides are also an opportunity for PBOT to test a more frequent bike bus schedule. The city says it will evaluate the program at the end of the season, including its frequency, routes, resources and staffing capacity, before deciding what changes to make for 2027.

For now, the special north and northeast bike buses continue with two more Wednesday rides through Oct. 14.

item.title: Washington state leaders raise alarm over plans to fast-track oil pipeline to Canada’s West Coast
item.dc:creator: Adia White
item.description: Washington leaders are speaking out about Canada’s plans to prioritize an oil pipeline from Alberta to British Columbia. They say it could have environmental consequences for the Pacific Northwest.
item.content:encoded:
Washington state leaders are warning that Canada’s decision to prioritize an oil pipeline from Alberta to British Columbia could have environmental consequences for the Pacific Northwest.

The pipeline would carry around 1 million barrels of oil a day to the British Columbia coast. The project, known as Pacific Link, is the first to be designated by Canada as being in the country’s national interest. The pipeline would bring oil to a new terminal south of Vancouver, British Columbia, that could accommodate large crude oil tankers for international shipping.

Gov. Bob Ferguson and Washington Department of Ecology Director Casey Sixkiller issued a joint news release Friday saying that prioritizing the project would fast-track it and limit environmental review. The two leaders warned it would bring more tankers carrying crude oil to the Salish Sea, which straddles the U.S.-Canada border, without a plan to respond to the possibility of catastrophic spills.

“Such a spill would pose an existential threat to the Southern Resident Killer Whales, to the unique ecosystems of the Salish Sea, and to the Tribal and First Nations communities that depend on these marine resources,” the two wrote in the joint statement.

Ferguson and Sixkiller said Canada needs to do more to ensure environmental stewardship of the two countries shared waters.

“Washington State has worked for decades to ensure that we are ready to respond to a major oil spill on either side of the border,” their statement said. “These existing resources would be insufficient in the face of this scale of expansion.”

The pipeline would reduce Canada’s dependence on U.S. trade and oil infrastructure. About 90% of Canadian oil is exported to the U.S. The pipeline could allow that oil to be sold in new markets in Asia.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said the pipeline would also create 140,000 jobs across the country and bring in about $100 billion in government revenue by 2060.

“Canada has a once-in-a-generation opportunity to become a global energy superpower,” Carney said in a news release Thursday. “To create hundreds of thousands of good jobs. To transform our economy. To diversify our trade. To become less reliant on a single trade partner.”

Carney said the goal is to complete the pipeline review process to clear the way for groundbreaking by September 2027.

item.title: Just short of its 200th birthday, a landmark natural history museum shuts down
item.dc:creator: Andrew Stelzer
item.description: Beloved for its dinosaurs, Philadelphia's storied Academy of Natural Sciences closed down this week, amid an intense fight by local residents, politicians and scientists to save it.
item.content:encoded:
Every weekend for the past month, the sidewalk in front of the Natural Academy of Sciences has simultaneously felt like a festival, a funeral, and a science fair.

On the Museum’s final Friday, there was a line of attendees waiting to get in; Activists circulating petitions and flyers to “Save the Academy”; and a museum educator showed off a giant salamander skull and a rare coat of pangolin scales.

For Philly area kids, visiting this place has been a rite of passage for generations. So when word dropped on September 1st that the nearly 200-year-old museum was closing at the end of the month, thousands of families began a wistful pilgrimage, to make one final visit.

“This is a very special place, for my family and also me growing up,” said Alexandria McCormick, who was visiting with her husband and six kids. She said when she was a child, her family used to come multiple times a year, awakening her love of natural history.

“It makes me really sad to think that my children might not also grow up having these experiences and being inspired to love nature this way.” she said.

Founded in 1812, and opened to the public in 1828, the Academy of Natural Sciences was the first place in the world to display a dinosaur skeleton, back in 1868. There’s also mammal dioramas, live animals, and other rotating exhibits.

Its collection of scientific specimens is widely recognized as one of the most important in the world. And its sudden demise comes amidst a continuing decline in funding for cultural and scientific institutions.

“This is the oldest natural history museum in the Americas,” says Isa Betancourt, who worked in the Academy’s entomology department for 10 years, from 2011 to 2021.

Betancourt now lives in Arizona, but hopped on a plane and came back to Philly to help organize the “Save the Academy” campaign, which included a flurry of rallies, marches, and an online petition to keep the museum open that has over 114,000 signatures.

“If this museum can slip away like that, what’s stopping other museums from going the same way? We can’t let this be a precedent.” she added.

A sudden closure

Drexel University, which took over financial responsibility for the Academy in 2011, explained on its website that post-pandemic, costs have risen and attendance declined. In its last few weeks, however, museum attendance skyrocketed and revenue was more than 20 times higher than last September.

“Maybe if they had announced this last year, they could have gotten the crowds they have now,” said Zoe Abrams, who was visiting with her husband and two children. “This is busier than Grand Central. Could have saved things.”

Some people working to save it criticized Drexel for not participating in any efforts to stem the museums’ closure, or providing details about how much it would cost to keep it open.

“When they announced the one month notice it was a surprise for everybody,” said Betancourt. “It’s like the leadership didn’t even try to keep it open, and that’s why there’s a lot of frustration around what’s happening. It’s just not right.” she added.

In response to a request for comment, Drexel said in a statement that it “remains deeply committed to protecting the Academy of Natural Sciences’ extraordinary legacy.”

Less than a week before the September 30th closing date, the William Penn Foundation offered a year’s worth of bridge funding; to buy time to explore more permanent solutions. Drexel said it is exploring the possibility of working with the foundation, but would need a plan for long-term sustainability before considering re-opening the museum.

Hard times for scientific institutions

The Academy houses a massive, irreplaceable library of over 19 million specimens. It includes Thomas Jefferson’s fossil collection, and plant samples gathered by Lewis and Clark. It also has an archive of 73,000 holotype specimens— carefully preserved samples which scientists use as references for defining and naming species.

Drexel has said it will preserve access to that collection for students and researchers. But it’s unclear what that means for the general public. And all this uncertainty comes at a moment when government support for cultural institutions has been in steep decline. “It’s certainly a challenging time for the museum field.” said Natanya Kashan, a spokesperson for the American Alliance of Museums. A 2025 survey of AAM’s members found a third had government grants and contracts cancelled, and more than two-thirds were affected by executive orders in some way.“The financial pressures are not only in federal funding, they’re also in philanthropy, in corporate donations, in individual giving,” she said.

The Academy tied its financial fate to Drexel’s, when, in 2011, the two institutions announced an “affiliation.” The Academy became a subsidiary of Drexel, but retained its own board and 501c3 organizational status. In a statement announcing the partnership the Academy’s president bragged about “a rock-solid balance sheet with a $51 million endowment”.

But, like many Universities, Drexel has been struggling financially, in part due to declining enrollment. In 2024, the school reported it was facing a budget shortfall.

And as attendance shrank, in 2025 the museum laid off some staff, and reduced its hours. It soon cancelled its 2026 summer camp program. Earlier this year, The Philadelphia Inquirer reported that the university and the Academy were renegotiating heir relationship; Drexel wanted a full merger, which would grant it the building, endowment and collections.

Amid speculation that Drexel plans to sell the 150-year-old building housing the Academy, Philadelphia’s city council proposed altering local zoning overlays in order to make selling the building or converting it to other uses more difficult. The council also plans to hold special public hearings, to find out how the Academy got to the point of closing, and what possible solutions might look like. The legislation calling for the hearing also gives the council subpoena power over Drexel.

“We need to know how this came to be. What were the levers that created this decision, and how do we undo that decision?” said City councilmember Dr. Nina Ahmad.

“There was no campaign in the recent past that we can find to encourage or to tell the city of Philadelphia, ‘We’re in danger of closing if you don’t come and use our museum.’ None of that.”

Philadelphia does have a track record of saving financially struggling cultural institutions, including the renowned Art collection at The Barnes Foundation, and the Please Touch Children’s Museum. But those campaigns took place before their respective museums closed. Reopening an already shuttered institution could be much more difficult.
